content.title: What does "jack" mean in slang?
content.text: In the U.S. it generally means “nothing”. Saying “you don't know jack” is saying “you don't know what you're talking about” or “you know nothing.” It is also used (by some) as an insulting way of telling someone that they mean so little to you that you can't be bothered to remember their real name…” Look, jack, I'm too busy to deal with you right now”, as an example. Replacing the person's real name with “jack” to belittle them.A multi-valued word, certainly…off the top of my head…A diminutive for John.A form of light armor (presumably from the same root as “jacket”).A drinking vessel made of leather.A term for people in general - often pejorative, implying the commonality. “He think’s Jack’s as good as his master.” Richard III’s lovely insult about “silken, sly insinuating jacks,” or a “jack in office” (someone with minor authority who abuses his position). But also “jack in the box” (a children’s toy where a little figure of a man pops out of a box).A lever device for raising a heavy weight (typically refers to a tool for elevating an automobile).an object in the game “jacks.” Little metal caltrops.slang for “nothing important” or an absence, eg. “jack shit” or simply jack is in “I’ve got jack.”coupled with “off,” a slang term for masturbation (usually male masturbation, given the mechanics of the act), possibly because it sounds like “jerk off.”I am sure I have missed some.That’s an interesting question. I always assumed Jack and Jacques were an informal form of Jacob. One of my grandfathers was a Jack, and this was also short for Jacob. But apparently this is the exception, not the rule— it is generally a short form of John. The explanation is that the medieval English used -kin as an affectionate ending, and so Jankin was shortened to Jack. Having said that, I wouldn’t be surprised if for many men nowadays, Jack is short for Jack, and that’s it. But evidently there’s an etymology for the word."Jack" in slang has several common meanings; context determines which applies. Key senses:Nothing / zeroExamples: "I know jack about that." = I know nothing. "You got jack" = you have nothing.Synonyms: squat, zilch, diddly.To stealExamples: "He got his phone jacked." = his phone was stolen. "They jacked the car." = they stole the car.Often used in past tense: jacked, jacking (rob/commandeer).To take by force / hijackExamples: "The truck was jacked on the highway." = forcibly taken; can imply violence.To increase / pump up (less common; chiefly in bodybuilding/athletic contexts)Examples: "He jacked up his bench press." = increased or intensified; "jacked" also means muscular.To remove / tamper withExamples: "They jacked the settings" = they messed with or altered them.To fool / con / swindle (regional)Example: "He got jacked out of his cash." = cheated out of.Usage notes:Tone ranges from casual to coarse; common in American English and many varieties.Collocations: "jack squat" (emphatic nothing), "jack up" (raise or wreck depending on context), "get jacked" (can mean get muscular or be robbed).Register: Informal; avoid in formal writing.Etymology snapshot:Likely from older senses of "jack" as a common noun for a man or tool; evolved into multiple verbs and emphatic uses over 20th century American slang.“Jack”, according to the Online Etymology Dictionary, is masculine proper name, attested by 1218, probably via Anglo-French Jake, Jaikes, from Old French Jacques (which was a diminutive of Latin Jacobus; see Jacob), but in English the name always has been regarded as a familiar form of John, and some have argued that it is a native formation. In Middle English spelled Jakke, Jacke, etc., and pronounced as two syllables ("Jackie"). Among American Jews, it tends to be a nickname for Jacob.My father was born in 1944 and his real first name is Jackie. He has always gone by Jack. Jackie is not short for anything, that’s what is on his birth certificate. He mother away passed giving birth to him so I don’t know why she picked that name for her son, but I like it. I have never met another man, or anyone for that matter, named Jackie, so this is probably rare. As mentioned before, I have more more commonly heard it related to the name “John”.One meaning is ‘alone'. It comes from the proper name ‘Jack Jones' and is used thusly: “I was all on me Jack", or “I was all on me Jack Jones". It is one of the few bits of Cockney rhyming slang which is not usually reduced to just the first word, however if one were to use just the first word the meaning would still be widely understood.“What does ‘yank’ mean in slang?” In the UK it means either “from the USA” or “pull sharply”.Jack is now a name used in its own right. But it used to be from John.Jason, Johannes. And from the French Jacques which is James in ,English.James the 1st of England liked being called Jacques, and that is where we get the flag the Union Jack (Jacgues/James).Not shorter but it is usually a nick name for John. My grandfather was a John known as Jack but it is now often used as a legal name.What is the meaning of the British slang word "Jack"?There’s a few meanings, so context would be helpful in decoding this. Off the top of my head: “I’m alright, Jack” - the attitude of one who cares only about their own wellbeing, even to the detriment of others. In other countries this might be called “pull up the drawbridge” or “fuck you, I’ve got mine”. “Jack-the-lad” - a brazen young man with a bit of a swagger about him, cocky and confident and up for a scrap. I believe it’s this meaning from which “Jack” entered lesbian slang for a butch woman, although this hasn’t been current for decades. “Man-jack” - only encountered in the set phrase “every man-jack”, ie, everyone. As with a lot of British slang, it has naval origins. Jack - a hill. Cockney rhyming slang, from “Jack and Jill”. To “jack (something) in” - to quit or stop partaking, particularly as of a job, but also “I’ve jacked in the smokes”.
